LT01T03.title: What a syllable is
LT01T03.focus: a syllable is one beat of a word, built around one vowel sound; you can feel the jaw open for each beat

LT01T03.title: Counting syllables
LT01T03.focus: count the vowel sounds you hear, not the letters you see: one, two or three beats
LT01T03.gloss: a very large animal with a trunk

LT01T03.title: Open and closed syllables
LT01T03.focus: a syllable that ends in a vowel is open and its vowel is long; one that ends in a consonant is closed and its vowel is short
LT01T03.gloss: a machine that can move and work

extra.gloss: to move from one place to another

LT01T03.title: The strong beat of a word
LT01T03.focus: in a word of two or more syllables one syllable is stronger: louder, longer and higher in pitch

LT01T03.title: Stress on the first syllable
LT01T03.focus: most two-syllable nouns and adjectives are stressed on the first syllable
LT01T03.gloss: a person who treats sick people

LT01T03.title: Stress on the second syllable
LT01T03.focus: many two-syllable words are stressed on the second syllable, and the first syllable becomes weak
LT01T03.gloss: a place to stay on a trip

LT01T03.title: Stress in long words
LT01T03.focus: in words of three or more syllables there is one strong beat and often a lighter second beat; the other syllables are weak
LT01T03.gloss: a person who helps for free

extra.gloss: the part of the day after noon

LT01T03.title: Stress that moves with the ending
LT01T03.focus: when a word gets a longer ending, the strong beat can move to another syllable
LT01T03.gloss: a picture made with a camera

LT01T03.title: Weak syllables and the schwa
LT01T03.focus: a weak syllable has a short, relaxed vowel called the schwa, the most common vowel sound in English

extra.gloss: a soft seat for two or more people
a person who helps you learn

LT01T03.title: Stress in compound words
LT01T03.focus: in a compound word made of two nouns the strong beat falls on the first part
LT01T03.gloss: a small brush for cleaning teeth

extra.gloss: a place where planes land and take off

LT01T03.title: Small unstressed words
LT01T03.focus: small grammar words such as and, of and to are usually weak: short, quiet and with a schwa
LT01T03.gloss: the word that joins two things

extra.gloss: the word that shows what something belongs to
the word that shows a direction

LT01T03.title: Syllables without a vowel
LT01T03.focus: in some words a final l or n makes its own syllable; the tongue stays in place and no vowel is said

extra.gloss: a small round fastener on clothes

LT01T04.title: Silent letters at the start
LT01T04.focus: at the start of some words the first letter is silent: k before n, w before r, g before n

extra.gloss: a small garden figure with a pointed hat

LT01T04.title: Silent b
LT01T04.focus: the letter b is silent after m at the end of a word and before t in a few words

LT01T04.title: Silent l
LT01T04.focus: the letter l is often silent between a vowel and k, f or m, as in walk, half and calm

LT01T04.title: Silent t
LT01T04.focus: the letter t is silent in some words, especially between s and l or n, and in often
LT01T04.gloss: to pay attention to a sound

LT01T04.title: Silent gh
LT01T04.focus: the letters gh are silent in many words, such as night, light and daughter

extra.gloss: the dark part of the day

LT01T04.title: Silent s
LT01T04.focus: the letter s is silent in a few words, such as island and aisle
LT01T04.gloss: land with water all around it

extra.gloss: a path between rows of seats

LT01T04.title: The silent e that makes a vowel long
LT01T04.focus: a silent e at the end of a word usually makes the vowel before it long: kit becomes kite
LT01T04.gloss: a toy that flies in the wind

extra.gloss: a set of tools or things

LT01T04.title: Double consonants keep the vowel short
LT01T04.focus: when a word gets an ending that starts with a vowel, a doubled consonant shows that the vowel before it is short: hopping, but hoping; the doubled consonant is said once, not twice, and it is not held longer

LT01T04.title: The ending -ed has three sounds
LT01T04.focus: the past ending -ed is said t after a voiceless sound, d after a voiced sound, and as a short extra syllable after t or d

extra.gloss: felt that you would like something

LT01T04.title: The ending -s has three sounds
LT01T04.focus: the ending -s depends on the last SOUND of the word, not the last letter: it is said s after a voiceless sound, z after a voiced sound, and as a short extra syllable after s, z, sh or ch sounds

LT01T04.title: Soft and hard c
LT01T04.focus: the letter c is usually said s before e, i or y and k before other letters

extra.gloss: a small container for a drink

cat.pt: um pequeno animal de estimação peludo
cat.ro: un mic animal de companie blănos

cup.en: a small container for a drink

LT01T04.title: Soft and hard g
LT01T04.focus: the letter g is often said like j before e, i or y and hard before other letters, but there are many exceptions

extra.gloss: a tall animal with a long neck

LT01T04.title: The t between vowels
LT01T04.focus: in American English a t between two vowel sounds is said as a quick tap of the tongue, like a soft d
LT01T04.gloss: a soft yellow food made from milk

LT01T04.title: Same sound, different spelling
LT01T04.focus: some words are said the same but spelled differently, so the spelling is what tells them apart

extra.gloss: the word that shows a direction

LT01T05.title: Contractions with be
LT01T05.focus: in speech, pronouns and the verb be join into one short word: I am becomes I'm, you are becomes you're, we are becomes we're

LT01T05.title: Negative contractions
LT01T05.focus: not joins the verb before it and becomes n't: do not becomes don't, is not becomes isn't

LT01T05.title: Can and can't
LT01T05.focus: can is usually weak and short with a schwa, while can't is strong with a clear vowel, so the vowel is what tells them apart; won't is an irregular short form of will not

LT01T05.title: The contraction 's
LT01T05.focus: the ending 's has three jobs: it can be is (he's), has (he's gone), or it shows who owns something (Sam's); it is said s or z, or with an extra syllable after s, z, sh or ch sounds

LT01T05.title: The contraction 'd
LT01T05.focus: the ending 'd can mean would or had, and the rest of the sentence shows which

I'd.ru: я бы или у меня было

she'd.ru: она бы или у неё было

they'd.ru: они бы или у них было

LT01T05.title: The contraction 'll
LT01T05.focus: the ending 'll is a short form of will and is said as a quick l after the pronoun

LT01T05.title: The contraction 've
LT01T05.focus: the ending 've is a short form of have and is said as a quick v; after could, would and should it is said as a weak extra syllable

LT01T05.title: Gonna, wanna and gotta
LT01T05.focus: in fast informal speech going to, want to and got to are said as gonna, wanna and gotta; they are spoken forms, not for formal writing

LT01T05.title: Weak forms of small words
LT01T05.focus: words such as for, was and have are usually said in a short weak form with a schwa, and only in a strong form when they are stressed or at the end of a sentence
LT01T05.gloss: the word that shows a purpose

LT01T05.title: Linking words together
LT01T05.focus: when a word ends in a consonant and the next word starts with a vowel, the two are joined and said as one smooth flow

LT01T05.title: Dropping the h in him and her
LT01T05.focus: in a sentence the h of him, her, his and have is often not said when the word is not stressed, so the word joins the one before it
LT01T05.gloss: to say something to a man

LT01T05.title: Would you and did you
LT01T05.focus: when a word ending in d or t meets you, the two sounds often join into a new one: would you sounds like wouldja, did you like didja

extra.gloss: the start of a question about the past
the start of a negative question

LT01T06.title: The beat of English rhythm
LT01T06.focus: English rhythm follows the strong beats: the time between strong beats stays about the same, so small words are squeezed when there are many of them
LT01T06.gloss: a short sentence with three strong beats

extra.gloss: the same three strong beats with small words added

extra.word: The dogs will like the bones
extra.gloss: still three strong beats with more small words

LT01T06.focus: in a sentence the main words, such as nouns, verbs and adjectives, are stressed, and small grammar words are weak

LT01T06.focus: in a normal statement the voice goes down on the last strong word and stays low at the end

LT01T06.focus: in a question that can be answered with yes or no the voice goes up at the end

LT01T06.focus: a question that starts with a question word such as what, where or why usually has a falling voice at the end, like a statement

LT01T06.title: The voice in a list
LT01T06.focus: in a list the voice rises a little after each item and falls on the last item, which tells the listener that the list is finished
LT01T06.gloss: three kinds of fruit in a list

LT01T06.title: Tag questions
LT01T06.focus: a tag question is a short question added to a statement; the voice goes up when you really ask and goes down when you expect the listener to agree

LT01T06.title: Stressing the important word
LT01T06.focus: you can make one word stronger, longer and higher than the others to show that it is the important one; this is how you choose between two things

LT01T06.title: Pauses between groups of words
LT01T06.focus: a speaker says a long sentence in short groups of words and takes a tiny pause between the groups; each group has its own strong beat and its own falling or rising voice

LT01T06.title: The full stop and the question mark
LT01T06.focus: the full stop shows a falling voice and the question mark shows a question; the same words can be a statement or a question, and the written mark and the voice tell you which

LT01T06.title: The exclamation mark
LT01T06.focus: an exclamation mark shows strong feeling: the voice is louder, with a wider and higher pitch on the important word
